source_text: Οὐδέποτε τῶν εἰς αὐτὸν ἁμαρτησάντων μέμνηται, ἀλλὰ ἀφίησι. διὸ καὶ δικαίως εὔχεται, »ἄφες ἡμῖν« λέγων· »καὶ γὰρ ἡμεῖς ἀφίεμεν·« ἓν γάρ ἐστι καὶ τοῦτο ὧν ὁ θεὸς βούλεται. μηδενὸς ἐπιθυμεῖν. μηδένα μισεῖν· ἑνὸς γὰρ θελήματος ἔργον οἱ πάντες ἄνθρωποι. καὶ μή τι τὸν γνωστικὸν »τέλειον« εἶναι βουλόμενος ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν »ὡς τὸν οὐράνιον πατέρα«. τουτέστιν ἑαυτόν. ὁ λέγων »δεῦτε. τέκνα. ἀκούσατέ μου φόβον κυρίου«, οὐ τῆς δι᾿ ἀγγέλων βοηθείας ἐπιδεῆ ἔτι εἶναι βούλεται τοῦτον, παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ δὲ ἄξιον γενόμενον λαμβάνειν. καὶ τὴν φρουρὰν ἔχειν παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ διὰ τῆς εὐπειθείας; ὁ τοιοῦτος ἀπαιτεῖ παρὰ κυρίου, οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ αἰτεῖ. καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πενομένων ἀδελφῶν οὐκ αὐτὸς αἰτήσεται ὁ γνωστικὸς [οὐ] χρημάτων περιουσίαν εἰς μετάδοσιν, ἐκείνοις δὲ ὧν δέονται χορηγίαν εὔξεται γενέσθαι. δίδωσι γὰρ οὕτως καὶ τὴν εὐχὴν τοῖς δεομένοις ὁ γνωστικὸς καὶ τὸ διὰ τῆς εὐχῆς ἀγνώστως ἅμα καὶ ἀτύφως παρέχεται. πενία μὲν οὖν πολλάκις καὶ νόσος καὶ τοιαῦται πεῖραι ἐπὶ νουθεσίᾳ προσφέρονται καὶ πρὸς διόρθωσιν τῶν παρεληλυθότων καὶ πρὸς ἐπιστροφὴν τῶν μελλόντων. ὁ τοιοῦτος τὸν ἐπικουφισμὸν τούτοις αἰτούμενος. ἅτε τὸ ἐξαίρετον τῆς γνώσεως ἔχων, οὐ διὰ κενοδοξίαν, ἀλλὰ δι᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ εἶναι γνωστικός, αὐτὸς ἐργάζεται τὴν εὐποιίαν. ὄργανον γενόμενος τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἀγαθότητος. Λέγουσι δὲ ἐν ταῖς παραδόσεσι Ματθίαν τὸν ἀπόστολον παρ᾿ ἕκαστα εἰρηκέναι ὅτι »ἐὰν ἐκλεκτοῦ γείτων ἁμαρτήσῃ, ἥμαρτεν ὁ ἐκλεκτός· εἰ γὰρ οὕτως ἑαυτὸν ἦγεν, ὡς ὁ λόγος ὑπαγορεύει, κατῃδέσθη ἂν αὐτοῦ τὸν βίον καὶ ὁ γείτων εἰς τὸ μὴ ἁμαρτεῖν«. τί τοίνυν περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ γνωστικοῦ φήσαιμεν ἄν; »ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε«, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος. »ὅτι ναός ἐστε τοῦ θεοῦ;« θεῖος ἄρα ὁ γνωστικὸς καὶ ἤδη ἅγιος, θεοφορῶν καὶ θεοφορούμενος. αὐτίκα τὸ ἁμαρτῆσαι ἀλλότριον παριστᾶσα ἡ γραφὴ τοὺς μὲν παραπεσόντας τοῖς ἀλλοφύλοις πιπράσκει· »μὴ ἐμβλέψῃς« δὲ »πρὸς ἐπιθυμίαν ἀλλοτρίᾳ γυναικὶ« λέγουσα. ἄντικρυς ἀλλότριον καὶ παρὰ φύσιν τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν λέγει. ναὸς δέ ἐστιν ὃ μὲν μέγας, ὡς ἡ ἐκκλησία, ὃ δὲ μικρός. ὡς ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ τὸ σπέρμα σῴζων τὸ Ἀβραάμ. οὐκ ἄρα ἐπιθυμήσει τινὸς ἑτέρου ὁ ἔχων ἀναπαυόμενον τὸν θεόν. αὐτίκα πάντα τὰ ἐμποδὼν καταλιπὼν καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν περισπῶσαν αὐτὸν ὕλην ὑπερηφανήσας τέμνει διὰ τῆς ἐπιστήμης τὸν οὐρανόν. καὶ διελθὼν τὰς πνευματικὰς οὐσίας καὶ πᾶσαν ἀρχὴν καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἅπτεται τῶν θρόνων τῶν ἄκρων, ἐπ᾿ ἐκεῖνο μόνον ἱέμενος, [ἐφ᾿] ὃ ἔγνω μόνον. μείξας οὖν τῇ περιστερᾷ τὸν ὄφιν τελείως ἅμα καὶ εὐσυνειδήτως βιοῖ, πίστιν ἐλπίδι κεράσας πρὸς τὴν τοῦ μέλλοντος ἀπεκδοχήν. αἴσθεται γὰρ τῆς δωρεᾶς ἧς ἔλαβεν ἄξιος γενόμενος τοῦ τυχεῖν, καὶ μετατεθεὶς ἐκ δουλείας εἰς υἱοθεσίαν. [ἀν] ἀκόλουθα τῇ ἐπιστήμῃ [μήτε μὴ] (»γνοὺς τὸν θεὸν [μᾶλλον δὲ] γνωσθείς τε πρὸς αὐτοῦ«) ἐπιτελεῖ, πρὸς ἀξίαν τῆς χάριτος ἐνδεικνύμενος τὰ ἐνεργήματα. ἕπεται γὰρ τὰ ἔργα τῇ γνώσει ὡς τῷ σώματι ἡ σκιά. Ἐπ᾿ οὐδενὶ τοίνυν εἰκότως ταράσσεται τῶν συμβαινόντων οὐδὲ ὑποπτεύει τῶν κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν ἐπὶ τῷ συμφέροντι γινομένων οὐδὲν οὐδὲ αἰσχύνεται ἀποθανεῖν, εὐσυνείδητος ὢν ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ὀφθῆναι, πάντας ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν τοὺς τῆς ψυχῆς ἀποκεκαθαρμένος σπίλους, ὅ γε εὖ μάλα ἐπιστάμενος ἄμεινον αὐτῷ μετὰ τὴν ἔξοδον γενήσεσθαι. ὅθεν οὐδέποτε τὸ ἡδὺ καὶ τὸ συμφέρον προκρίνει τῆς οἰκονομίας, γυμνάζων ἑαυτὸν διὰ τῶν ἐντολῶν, ἵνα καὶ πρὸς τὸν κύριον εὐάρεστος ἐν πᾶσι γένηται καὶ πρὸς τὸν κόσμον ἐπαινετός. ἐπεὶ τὰ πάντα ἐφ᾿ ἑνὸς τοῦ παντοκράτορος θεοῦ ἵσταται. »εἰς τὰ ἴδια«. φησίν, »ἦλθεν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ οἱ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν οὐκ ἐδέξαντο.« διὸ καὶ κατὰ τὴν τῶν κοσμικῶν χρῆσιν οὐ μόνον εὐχαριστεῖ καὶ θαυμάζει τὴν κτίσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ χρώμενος ὡς προσῆκεν ἐπαινεῖται. ἐπεὶ τὸ τέλος αὐτῷ δι᾿ ἐνεργείας γνωστικῆς τῆς κατὰ τὰς ἐντολὰς εἰς θεωρίαν περαιοῦται. ἐνθένδε ἤδη, δι᾿ ἐπιστήμης τὰ ἐφόδια τῆς θεωρίας καρπούμενος μεγαλοφρόνως τε τὸ τῆς γνώσεως ἀναδεξάμενος μέγεθος, πρόεισιν ἐπὶ τὴν ἁγίαν τῆς μεταθέσεως ἀμοιβήν. ἀκήκοεν γὰρ τοῦ ψαλμοῦ λέγοντος· »κυκλώσατε Σιὼν καὶ περιλάβετε αὐτήν, διηγήσασθε ἐν τοῖς πύργοις αὐτῆς« αἰνίσσεται γάρ. οἶμαι. τοὺς ὑψηλῶς προσδεξαμένους τὸν λόγον ὑψηλοὺς ὡς πύργους ἔσεσθαι καὶ βεβαίως ἔν τε τῇ πίστει καὶ τῇ γνώσει στήσεσθαι.
pass_a_gloss: He never remembers those who have sinned against him, but forgives. Therefore, he also prays justly, saying 'Forgive us' and 'for we also forgive.' For this is one of the things that God wills: to desire nothing, to hate no one. For the work of one will is for all people. And our Savior, wanting the gnostic to be 'perfect' as the heavenly Father, that is, Himself, says 'Come, children, listen to me, fear of the Lord.' He does not want this one to be in need of help through angels, but to be worthy to receive it from Himself. And to have a guard through obedience? Such a person demands from the Lord, not asks. And for the poor brothers, the gnostic will not ask for a abundance of wealth to give to them, but will pray to become a provision for them of the things they need. For the gnostic gives a prayer to those in need and provides through prayer, unknowingly and humbly. Therefore, poverty and disease and such trials are often offered for instruction and for correction of past things and for a return to future things. Such a person, having the exceptional thing of knowledge, not through vain glory, but through being gnostic, works the good deed, becoming an instrument of God's goodness. They say in the traditions that Matthew the apostle said concerning each thing, 'If a neighbor of the elect sins, the elect has sinned; for if he had conducted himself thus, as the word dictates, he would have been a warning to his neighbor not to sin.' What then shall we say about the gnostic? 'Or do you not know,' says the apostle, 'that you are a temple of God?' The gnostic is therefore divine and already holy, bearing God and being borne by God. The scripture immediately presents sin as alien, selling those who have fallen to the aliens. Saying 'do not look' at an alien woman's desire, it says that sin is alien and against the nature of the temple of God. The temple is both great, as the church, and small, as the person who keeps the seed of Abraham. The one who has God resting in him will not desire anything else. Immediately, having left all hindrances and having overcome all the matter that distracts him, he cuts through the heaven through knowledge. And having passed through the spiritual substances and all authority and power, he touches the highest thrones, striving for only that which he has known. Having mixed the dove with the serpent, he lives perfectly and with a good conscience, having crowned faith with hope for the expectation of the future. For he is aware of the gift which he has received, having become worthy to obtain it, and having been transferred from slavery to adoption. Following the knowledge, he completes the works worthy of the grace, showing the deeds. For the works follow knowledge as the shadow follows the body. Therefore, he is not disturbed by anything that happens, nor does he suspect anything that occurs for the benefit according to the economy, nor is he ashamed to die, being conscious of having been seen by the authorities, having purified all the stains of the soul. Knowing well that it will be better for him after his departure, he does not choose the pleasant and the beneficial over the economy, training himself through the commandments, so that he may be pleasing to the Lord in all things and praised by the world. Since all things depend on the one almighty God, he says 'the Son of God came to his own, and his own did not receive him.' Therefore, he not only gives thanks and marvels at the creation according to the use of worldly things, but also, using them as is fitting, he is praised. For his goal is to pass through the gnostic activity according to the commandments to contemplation. From here, already, through knowledge, he plucks the provisions of contemplation, having taken on the magnitude of knowledge in a great-minded way, he proceeds to the holy reward of transfer. For he has heard the psalm saying, 'Surround Zion and encircle it, tell it in its towers.' I think he praises those who have received the word in a high way, to be high as towers and to stand firmly in both faith and knowledge.

pass_b_english: He never recalls those who have sinned against him; he simply forgives them. That is why he can pray justly, saying, "Forgive us, for we also forgive" — because forgiving is one of the very things God wills: to desire nothing, to hate no one, since all humanity is the work of a single divine will. And our Savior, wanting the gnostic to be "perfect as the heavenly Father" (Matt. 5:48) — that is, Himself — says, "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord" (Ps. 34:11). He does not intend the gnostic still to need help mediated through angels, but to become worthy of receiving aid directly from Himself. And is the gnostic to have a guard through obedience? Such a person demands this from the Lord; he does not merely ask. Even on behalf of needy brothers, the gnostic will not petition for a surplus of wealth to distribute, but will pray to become himself the provision of whatever they lack. For the gnostic gives his prayer to those in need, and through that prayer supplies their want unknowingly and without pride.

Therefore poverty, sickness, and similar trials are often brought as instruction, for the correction of past failures and for the return to a right path in the future. The gnostic, who possesses the distinctive gift of knowledge, seeks relief from these afflictions not from vainglory but simply because he is a gnostic; and so he himself works the good, becoming an instrument of God's goodness. The traditions report that the apostle Matthew said of each situation: "If a neighbor of the elect sins, the elect has sinned; for if he had conducted himself as the Word dictates, his neighbor would have been restrained from sinning by the warning of his life." What then shall we say of the gnostic himself? "Do you not know that you are a temple of God?" (1 Cor. 3:16), says the apostle. The gnostic is therefore divine and already holy, bearing God and borne by God. Scripture immediately presents sin as something alien, handing over those who have fallen to the aliens, and saying, "Do not look with desire upon an alien woman" (cf. Prov. 6:25); it declares sin to be utterly alien and contrary to the nature of the temple of God. The temple is both great, as the Church, and small, as the person who guards the seed of Abraham. Hence the one who has God resting in him will not desire anything else. At once he leaves behind every hindrance and, rising above all the matter that distracts him, cuts through the heavens by means of knowledge. Passing through the spiritual substances and every rule and authority, he touches the highest thrones, straining toward that alone which he has known. Having blended the dove with the serpent, he lives perfectly and with a clear conscience, weaving faith with hope toward the expectation of what is to come.

For he is aware of the gift he has received, having become worthy to obtain it and having been transferred from slavery into adoption. Walking in step with knowledge, he fulfills the works worthy of grace, displaying the deeds; for works follow knowledge as the shadow follows the body. Consequently he is not disturbed by anything that happens, nor does he suspect any event that occurs for his benefit within the divine economy; he is not even ashamed to die, conscious that he will appear before the authorities with a clear conscience, having cleansed every stain from his soul. Knowing full well that it will be far better for him after his departure, he never prefers the pleasant or the immediately advantageous over the economy, but trains himself through the commandments so that he may be well-pleasing to the Lord in all things and commended even by the world. Since all things stand fast upon the one Almighty God, he says, "The Son of God came to his own, and his own did not receive him" (John 1:11). Therefore, in his use of worldly things he not only gives thanks and marvels at creation, but by using them as he ought he is himself commended. For his goal is to advance through gnostic activity according to the commandments into contemplation. From this point onward, harvesting the provisions for contemplation through knowledge and embracing the magnitude of knowledge with greatness of soul, he presses on toward the holy reward of transference. For he has heard the psalm saying, "Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers" (Ps. 48:12–13); this means, I think, that those who have received the Word in a lofty way will become lofty as towers and will stand firm in both faith and knowledge.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a polished version with appropriate scripture citations (Matt 5:48, Ps 34:11, 1 Cor 3:16, Prov 6:25, John 1:11, Ps 48:12-13) that correspond to the Greek allusions and quotations. The distinction between 'demanding' (ἀπαιτεῖ) and 'asking' (αἰτεῖ) is preserved. The complex theological descriptions of the gnostic's ascent and the relationship between knowledge and works are handled correctly.
